questions.question: Explain the political results of British colonisation for the Asante.
questions.expected_answer: After 1901 the Asante lost their independence and were ruled by a Chief Commissioner in Kumasi under the Gold Coast governor; the Asantehene was in exile, the Asante union was broken up and Britain controlled laws, taxes, courts, police, army and recognition of chiefs. Under indirect rule chiefs collected taxes, kept order and settled disputes under district commissioners, and could be destooled by the government, which changed chieftaincy from accountability to communities to accountability to British officials and caused tensions. Prempeh I returned in 1924 and was recognised as Kumasihene in 1926, and in 1935 Britain restored the Asante Confederacy with Prempeh II as Asantehene, recognising Asante identity and using it for indirect rule. The Golden Stool stayed in Asante hands after the British promised not to interfere in 1921. Asante was governed with the Gold Coast Colony, the Northern Territories and British Togoland and became part of Ghana, though in the 1950s the National Liberation Movement sought a federal system.

questions.question: Describe the economic results of colonisation in Asante and the Gold Coast.
questions.expected_answer: Cocoa, introduced by Tetteh Quarshie in 1879 and Basel missionaries, was planted on a large scale by African farmers on their own land, using family and hired migrant labour; some became wealthy and by about 1911 the Gold Coast was the world's largest producer, with government revenue depending on cocoa. European trading companies controlled prices and in the 1930s kept them low, leading to the cocoa hold-up of 1937 to 1938, and dependence on one crop left the colony vulnerable to price falls and swollen shoot disease. The Ashanti Goldfields Corporation, founded in 1897, mined at Obuasi with African migrant labour in hard conditions, sending profits to Britain, and manganese, diamonds and bauxite were also mined. Railways ran from Sekondi to Tarkwa and Kumasi by 1903 and from Accra to Kumasi by 1923, with Takoradi harbour in 1928 and roads with African-owned lorries, all mainly for exports. Revenue came from customs duties, forced labour was used, and the north was treated as a labour reserve.

questions.question: Describe the social results of colonisation and explain how the Gold Coast won independence, and the results for Britain.
questions.expected_answer: Missions such as the Basel Mission, Methodists and Catholics built schools and churches and many Asante became Christian; Governor Guggisberg expanded education and opened Achimota College in 1927, but secondary and higher education stayed limited, especially in the north. Hospitals were mainly in towns; Kumasi grew into a major commercial city; cocoa created prosperous farmers, traders, lorry owners and professionals, while northern migrants did hard labour and regional inequality grew. Grievances over political exclusion, cocoa prices, import prices, unemployment and racism united the educated, farmers, workers, ex-servicemen and chiefs after the Second World War: the UGCC was founded in 1947 with Nkrumah as secretary, police fired on ex-servicemen in Accra in February 1948, Nkrumah founded the CPP in 1949 demanding self-government now, won the 1951 election and led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana on 6 March 1957, the first in sub-Saharan Africa. Britain gained cocoa, gold, timber, profits, markets and prestige, bore costs of wars and administration, and kept ties through the Commonwealth.
